_what: Real exposures of distant solar-system objects for the find-the-moving-object game, fetched from the telescope archives and aligned on the stars by scripts/fetch_game_sequences.py, with the object's position in every frame computed from the Minor Planet Center's records and checked against the pixels.
_positions: Pixels in the saved frame: origin at the top-left corner, x right, y down, pixel centres at +0.5. times are mid-exposure, UT.

skipped.why: too faint to follow by eye: its discovery night's nine 287-s MegaCam exposures (OSSOS, 29 September 2013) show it at r = 24 to 25, three to four times the noise in each, and most are too far apart in time to add

too faint to follow by eye: on its best-covered night (10 October 2013, thirteen 330-s DECam z exposures in a Dark Energy Survey supernova field) it stands two to five times above the noise even with exposures added in pairs, and its track runs past a brighter galaxy
too faint to follow by eye: its discovery night (18 February 2015, five 86-s DECam g exposures of the HiTS survey, 1.6 hours apart) shows it at g = 24, four to five times the noise in each
too faint to follow by eye: on 17 May 2015 (five 300-s MegaCam exposures, OSSOS) it is at r = 24.5 to 25, about three times the noise in each

its discovery night (26 March 2014) has only three DECam exposures; the archive's other nights with five or more in one filter (DECam, March 2016) last twenty minutes, in which it moves under three pixels, and the MPC has no positions from them
the Dark Energy Survey imaged it once or twice a night, each time in a different filter (21 October 2014: r, i, z, z), so no night has five exposures in one filter
